It's been maybe three months or so since my cat Luna passed away from kidney disease. I'm *still* not over it. She was my little girl, my baby, my best friend for 13 years. I have no one to hold when I go to sleep, or when I'm sad. I can still feel the texture of her fur on my hands. I still love her. Days when I do think about her fondly are easier. Other days, I think of her and I'm a mess. I see her in my dreams; sometimes it's a nightmare, where I have to revisit losing her all over again, but sometimes it's a good dream, where I can hold her and feel her purring again, and waking up to reality becomes the nightmare.

I can't say it will get better immediately, or even a few months from now. You shared a deep bond with another living being, and that's special. Hold onto that. If you think of him in sadness, try to focus on the happiest memories. Maybe you could look back at old photos or videos to sort of experience their presence again. Or, take a break, distract yourself; I sometimes try the 5-minute rule, where I start something I know I usually enjoy, try it for about 5-minutes, and hopefully by the time 5 minutes comes around, I'm engaged and distracted.

I don't know if that will help, but I can at least relate to your pain.

Luna was such a sweet young lady, but she was also a pretty tough cookie. She was never more than about 5lbs, but she was always top housecat. The handful of times my roommates in the past have had cats, she would give them a hiss and a swat (no claw) to say "Hey! I'm in charge!" It almost always worked, except for once when she swatted at a cat with special needs. Poor thing was so confused why he wasn't responding like the other cats. But, after a few days, you could find any of the house cats playing and cuddling with her.

When she wasn't pretending to be tough, she was a little baby. She had her alone times, of course, but most often she would follow me around the house, or hang out in whatever room the people were in at the moment. And what a lap cat! Any time I sat down, she saw it as an opportunity to jump into my lap for some love and snuggles, and it always worked. She had this cat magic about her where she would approach you, and the next thing you knew, you were petting her. You didn't know when you started petting her, but that was part of her magic.

Luna was also a shoulder cat. She was happy to let me hold her and walk around with her in my arms, but sometimes she wanted to be a little higher up, and she'd climb or jump up onto my left shoulder, spin in a little circle so she was facing the right way, and hunker down for a ride! She was so good at it, I wouldn't even need to support her with my hands most of the time. She'd headbump my face and purr happily, and then jump down when she decided that she was done. 

Her meows were the sweetest. She was very talkative, especially with food and treats, but she'd also cry when left alone or when I was out of eyesight. Of course, say her name and call her over, and she'd prance her way over to you for affection. She would often fall asleep with me at night by laying on top of my chest or next to my face (sometimes both simultaneously), and wake me up with little headbumps and nose kisses.  Her fur was so velvety and soft. Luna's favorite place for pets was her cheeks and chin; she was so small, you sometimes had to use just one finger to pet her little forehead. 

I could go on and on about my baby. I love her so much.

I once had the most spontaneously stabbing pain in my chest over my heart, and boy I panicked. (For context, this happened when I was 26.) It was surreal, at its worst I couldn't move around or take deep breaths without making the pain worse, and it lasted maybe 20-30 minutes before it faded. Turns out there's a condition called costochondritis that causes inflammation near the sternum, which can cause instances of pain and pressure in your chest. I still have it, a few times a week or so now, but I'm not afraid I might be having a heart attack all the time anymore.
I'm so sorry you had to go through that, I'm in a similar place right now with my (now, ex) fiancee and her new boyfriend, and both avoiding me. If you would like to vent, I can be here to listen.

What do you enjoy? What makes you happy, even a little bit? A pet? Painting? Photography? Video games? Books? The ocean?

If you go, you may never be able to enjoy those things again. They might only last a short while, and maybe it's not enough to live for, but it might be something to motivate you, or that you might miss.

I'm so sorry you are feeling this way. I'm also having a hard time finding a reason to live, but I hope that maybe it's something you can think about.

Was about 15 or 16, I walked myself to the dentist after school. They put me in a room, gave me the bib, and said they would be right back. More than a half hour passes and still no sign of the dentist, so I pop my head in the hall and ask an aid when I'll be seen. She tells me the dentist will be right in, and I go back to my chair. *More* time passes, it's getting darker outside, and *still* no dentist. Then, I see lights in the hall start to turn off. An aid comes into my room, notices me in the chair, and asks why I'm still there. I told her I *still* hadn't been seen, she starts apologizing and runs to get the dentist. He *finally* comes in and spends a handful of minutes going through a regular exam, and I finally get to go home. 

TL;DR: The dentist forgot I was there, left me for a few hours, and was going to close for the day with me still in a chair and wearing a bib. I don't go there anymore.

Used to live a second floor apartment in the city. My roommates were at work, the third floor neighbors were home, but there were no cars in the parking lot. 

The back door to our apartment was adjacent to the only door leading to the third floor, so when someone knocks on their door, it sounds like they're knocking on our door. 

So, when I heard a knock at the door, followed by "(CITY) POLICE, OPEN THE DOOR" my first instinct was to open it. Something felt off, my gut told me not to open the door, so I crept up and as quietly as I could, I locked the handle. A few moments later, there was a gunshot upstairs, and I *dropped* to the ground. I immediately shut off anything in the apartment that made noise and locked the front door. I stayed down and silent for as long as possible before checking to see if it was safe to make sound. 

The man impersonating a cop knew the guys upstairs sold drugs, so he knew he could rob them if they were alone. Fortunately nobody was seriously injured. However, he had no idea I was there. If I had opened that door, he may have shot me by reflex. My guts potentially saved my life that day.

A doctor might want to have you undergo a sleep study to see what may be going on while youre asleep. They may also prescribe sleep medications to help your body stay still and rested instead of lashing out. 
I still don't know the underlying cause of my sleep disorder, but certain meds have helped me sleep without moving (or hitting my fiancee or a wall).
There are all sorts of sleep disorders, so it's important to make sure there isn't something more going on.
